title: Huo, Ling, Wang, Zhou 2026 - Heterogeneity: A multi-robot radioactive source search technique (Progress in Nuclear Energy 193, 106223)

q.Q1: Implicit, unquantified cap on time steps, not a dose budget. Sec 3.1: 'K denotes the upper limit of the mobile robot's residence time in the radiation environment, which is constrained by its radiation resistance level.' In Sec 5 this becomes a fixed termination rule: 'particle convergence of the mobile robot or a total number of radiation detections exceeding 30.' No tolerance in Gy is given for any robot, and no cumulative dose is tracked. Exposure is kept low only indirectly: 'To limit computational time and to avoid prolonged exposure of the robot to the radiation environment, the decision-making algorithm adopted in this paper uses an approximate form of FID' (Sec 4.3), and 'to limit radiation exposure of the mobile robot, only the rewards for the decision set A = {S; up, down, left, right} are evaluated' (Sec 5). Fig. 7 counts detections, which the authors present as a stand-in for exposure: 'reduces the total radiation exposure experienced by the mobile robot.'
q.Q2: Not found in the text. There is no exit, return path, reserve or withdrawal. The mobile robot ends at the source: 'the mobile robot ultimately moves to the source location to complete the search task' (Sec 5), and 'When the variances are small ... moves directly toward the estimated source position' (Sec 4.3).
q.Q3: No. Nothing about dose is predicted. The source estimate drives only information gain: 'the FID is computed based on the current fixed source estimate' (Sec 4.3), so it uses a point estimate, not the particle spread. Particle variance only shrinks the step size (Eq. 21). There is no pessimism or percentile. Source activity is assumed known: 'the searchers know only the size of the area and the activity of the radioactive source' (Sec 4).
q.Q4: 3 robots with fixed, hand-designed roles. 'Two fixed robots with lower radiation resistance are positioned at the edge ... a mobile robot with high radiation resistance enters the warning area' (Abstract). Fixed robots sit at [0,0] and [0,200] m and take 800 measurements each; the mobile robot starts at [0,100] m (Sec 5). Roles follow from radiation resistance, which is a qualitative label: 'these robots are exposed to lower radiation levels and therefore require only limited radiation resistance' (Sec 5). Roles are never reallocated online. Coordination is one-way and sequential: the fixed robots' NG-MLE estimate seeds the mobile robot's particle filter (Eq. 14).
q.Q5: Fixed robots run NG-MLE (natural-gradient MLE) on long-range Poisson data and intersect two range circles. The mobile robot runs a particle filter over (xs, ys) only, with a biased prior (particles drawn within +/-10 m of the fixed-robot estimate when kappa<0.2), plus a greedy FID next-best-view over 4 directions with an adaptive step. Environment: 2D, obstacle-free, 200x200 m, Is = 2.94e8 Bq, 1 cps background, 50 Monte Carlo trials. Results: NG-MLE error 5.93 m vs 77.61 m for a standard-gradient MLE (Table 1). The full method's mean error is 0.29 m with 750 particles and 1.38 m with 125, vs 1.46 / 5.63 m for PF+entropy and 0.94 / 7.97 m for PF+free energy (Table 2). It also needs fewer detections (Fig. 7).
q.Q7: Element (1): partial and only implicit. A resistance-limited residence time K is mentioned but implemented as a 30-detection cap, with no dose accounting or Gy values. (2): no. (3): no. The estimate feeds only information gain, and activity is assumed known. (4): partial. Heterogeneous radiation tolerance determines roles, but roles are fixed in advance, there are no budgets, no online risk sharing and no withdrawal.

stated_gaps.text: Obstacle-free 2D plane; no scattering or attenuation
stated_gaps.quote: This paper assumes an obstacle-free scenario and ignores the effects of time variation, scattering, and medium absorption.

stated_gaps.text: Source activity known; only position is estimated
stated_gaps.quote: the searchers know only the size of the area and the activity of the radioactive source, while the specific position of the source is unknown.

stated_gaps.text: Sensor layout and data volume vs. accuracy (Cramér-Rao bound)
stated_gaps.quote: Future work will examine the effects of radiation sensor layout and detection data volume on localization accuracy, which may be associated with the Cramér–Rao bound in information theory.

stated_gaps.text: Mobile strategies for sparse far-field data
stated_gaps.quote: To address the common issue of sparse detections in regions far from the source, further research will focus on how mobile strategies can improve data acquisition and localization performance.

stated_gaps.text: Radiation resistance is never quantified (no Gy), and the residence limit K is a fixed detection count, not a dose-based budget. No exit, no robot-level dose accounting.
Roles (static low-tolerance vs. mobile high-tolerance) are assigned by design. With one mobile robot there is no coordination or risk sharing between robots that enter the hazard zone.
Simulation only. The mobile robot ends at the source with no notion of surviving the mission.

thesis_relevance: The closest prior work on 'robots differ in radiation tolerance, so assign who enters the hot zone'. It does this with static roles, an unquantified tolerance and a step cap, so the thesis's quantified per-robot budget, exit reserve, estimate-based dose prediction and online risk sharing are all absent.

title: Ling, Huo, Moiseev, Hu, Xiao 2022 - Multi-robot collaborative radioactive source search based on particle fusion and adaptive step size (Annals of Nuclear Energy 173, 109104)

q.Q1: Ignored. The robots' own dose and any resource limit do not appear. The only safety motivation concerns humans: robots 'can effectively avoid the radiation damage of the technicians' (Sec 1). Episodes end on success: 'This process cycle continues until the radioactive source is searched.' (Sec 4).
q.Q2: Not found in the text. Success requires every robot to end near the source: 'the distance between all robots and the real source is less than 40 m' (Sec 5).
q.Q3: No dose prediction. The particle-filter estimate of A=(X,Y,I) feeds only the free-energy reward and the adaptive step: 'S is related to the estimated distance from the current position to the source and the variance of the particle distribution' (Sec 4). Particle variance makes motion cautious for estimation reasons, not for dose: 'when the source uncertainty increases, it is switched to cautious action mode by reducing the step size' (Sec 5.2).
q.Q4: 4 homogeneous robots (GM detectors), decentralized. Each runs its own PF, fuses others' measurements weighted by KL-based 'cognitive difference', and swaps the h highest-weight particles into neighbours' sets (Algorithm 1). 'Each robot chooses the next action based on the reward value in its own action set' (Sec 4). No roles, no heterogeneity, no risk allocation.
q.Q5: PF over position and intensity, with measurement fusion, particle fusion, and a free-energy (infotaxis-to-exploitation) policy with adaptive step. Environment: 2D, barrier-free, 900x900 m, I = 3e9 Bq, simulation only. Results: measurement fusion takes success from 65% to 100% and MST from 61.95 to 32.45 (Table 1). With particle fusion, 4 robots x 100 particles reach 96% success in 9 s, vs 94% in 104 s for 4x1000 and 63% for 1 robot x 1000 (Table 2). Adaptive step gives MST 17.26 and SR 94%, vs fixed S=20 at SR 92% and MST 49.1, and S=100 at SR 2% (Sec 5.2).
q.Q7: None of (1)-(4). Homogeneous, dose-agnostic multi-robot PF search. Relevant only as the shared-belief, multi-robot PF baseline that the thesis extends.

stated_gaps.text: Real experiments; deep RL for parameter optimization; obstacles; avoiding repeated search and collisions
stated_gaps.quote: Future works will include verifying the proposed algorithm in real experiments and utilizing deep reinforcement learning to solve parameter optimization problems. Further, radioactive source search in obstacle environments and avoiding repeated searches and collisions will be explored.

stated_gaps.text: Barrier-free 2D space; fixed source
stated_gaps.quote: Two-dimensional barrier-free space: W = 900m x 900m; The location and activity of the lost radioactive source are fixed throughout the search process

stated_gaps.text: Timing ignores robot motion
stated_gaps.quote: only the time required for the algorithm operation is considered without considering the time required for moving the robot.

stated_gaps.text: No robot dose, survivability or exit modeled. Success is defined by all robots converging on the source, which is the opposite of dose-aware behaviour.

thesis_relevance: A representative dose-agnostic multi-robot PF search from the same group. It supplies the baseline paradigm (shared/fused particle belief over position and activity) and explicitly names deep RL and obstacles as future work, both of which the thesis adopts.

title: Alagha, Singh, Mizouni, Bentahar, Otrok 2022 - Target localization using Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning with Proximal Policy Optimization (FGCS 136, 342-357)

q.Q1: Soft cost in a shared reward, about movement and not about dose. Eq. 4: R_t = 1-b if the team got closer, else -1-b, 'where b is the number of agents who took a moving action ... The term (-b) ... represents the cost of movement' (Sec 4). 'Cost could be in terms of power consumption or incentives paid to individuals' (Sec 3.1). There are no per-agent budgets: 'We do not focus on the different types of resource consumption in this work, and assume each agent has 1 cost unit if decided to take a moving action' (Sec 5.2.5).
q.Q2: No exit or return. The closest behaviour is learned idling to save cost: agents 'are expected to become idle at some point to save resources, given that other agents have more informative readings' (Sec 3.1). In Sec 5.2.4, Agent 2 'decides to stay idle after one exploration step'. This is stopping, not leaving the area.
q.Q3: No. There is no source estimator at all; the policy reads heatmaps of readings and visit counts. Readings are CPM proportional to I/d^2 with background ignored (Eq. 5). No dose prediction, no pessimism.
q.Q4: 1-4 and 10 homogeneous agents with a shared actor (CLDE: centralized critic, decentralized execution). Behaviour (splitting, idling) emerges from the team reward; there are no explicit roles. The Bayesian baseline [18] (Xiao et al. 2017, 'cooperative multiagent online search with resource constraints') does balance resources across agents. In that baseline 'some agents could be of use to the localization task, but decide not to move if the amount of resources they have is much less than the average of the team' (Sec 5.2.5). This is the only text in these five papers that touches allocation under unequal budgets.
q.Q5: PPO with CNN actor/critic over 2D maps. Three models: CMTL (joint), DMTL (shared actor, central critic) and ODMTL (windowed plus downsampled maps). Environment: 1x1 km on a 10x10 grid, 5 actions, target strength 1e9 photons/min, no obstacles; an episode ends when an agent enters the target cell or after 100 steps. Results: DMTL/ODMTL reach 100% success at all team sizes, while CMTL falls to 45% at 4 agents. The 3-agent ODMTL costs 7.9% less than single-agent DDQN. Against baselines it is up to 2.9x faster than DDQN-2, 58% faster with 62% less cost than Bayesian, and 3x faster with 87% less cost than uniform search (Sec 5.2.5).
q.Q7: (1): no. Movement cost is a soft shared penalty, not a per-robot hard budget. (2): no. Idling is not withdrawal or exit. (3): no. (4): partial only through emergent idling in a homogeneous team. The unequal-resource balancing appears only in a cited baseline [18].

stated_gaps.text: Obstacles affecting movement and readings
stated_gaps.quote: The complexity of the environment is to be further increased, through introducing obstacles that could hinder the movement of the agents and affect their readings.

stated_gaps.text: Restricted communication
stated_gaps.quote: communication between agents should be restricted, to increase the realism of the proposed models.

stated_gaps.text: Federated RL for physical-world learning
stated_gaps.quote: recent works on Federated RL [54] could prove efficient in handling distributed learning, which could be suitable for localization systems where the learning occurs in the physical world.

stated_gaps.text: Background ignored; single target
stated_gaps.quote: The background radiation is ignored since it is negligible when compared to the radioactive target.

stated_gaps.text: Shared-policy symmetry breaks cooperation when agents are co-located
stated_gaps.quote: each agent has the same copy of the actor network, and hence both would end up taking the same action.

stated_gaps.text: Success is defined as stepping into the source cell, which is lethal for a strong gamma source. No dose model, no per-agent budget, no estimator-based risk.

thesis_relevance: The main MAPPO-style MARL precedent for radiation source localization. It shows that cost-aware cooperation (idling) can emerge from a team reward, but treats cost as a soft movement penalty with no dose, budget, exit or source belief, which is exactly the gap the thesis fills.

title: Zhao, Wang, Zhang, Chen 2014 - gamma Ray irradiation test of control system of nuclear emergency rescue robot (IEEE ICIST)

q.Q1: An empirical hardware failure threshold, not a planning budget. 'the control system and communication link survived under 100Gy' (Abstract). Table V lists the total doses at which components became abnormal or incapable: serial bus communication 130 Gy (abnormal); network communication 270-280 Gy (incapable); EEPROM 256 Gy (abnormal). Conclusion: 'when total dose exceeded 400Gy EEPROM could not write.' Target: 'control system can survived under the total dose 100Gy total dose which was the target of our typical robotic joint [2]' (Sec IV.C).
q.Q2: Not found in the text (not a planning paper).
q.Q3: Not applicable. The doses were measured with alanine dosimeters, and the dose at failure was estimated from timing: 'we could not acquire the dose ralue exactly, we gave a rough dose value estimation based on the timing of events' (Sec IV.C).
q.Q4: Not applicable. Three Arduino Ethernet test systems in different power modes (A always on, B rebooted every 10 min, C never powered) plus a memory-test platform. Finding: 'the control system which did not work survived longer than the working one, rebooting can enhance the ability of control system to survive' (Sec IV.C).
q.Q5: Co-60 irradiation at the China Institute of Atomic Energy. Line-shaped Co-60 sources were raised from a 7 m pool; platforms sat at 1.2 m height. Schedule: about 50 Gy/h for 2 h (100 Gy), then 100 Gy/h for 1 h (200 Gy), then 200 Gy/h for 1 h, for a theoretical total of 400 Gy over 4 h. Events: serial-bus 'messy codes' at 116 Gy (2 h 10 min), worsening by 200 Gy. Network loss 'When reaching to 200Gy/h' for system A, with system B lost 15 min later. EEPROM write errors at 256 Gy (3 h 6 min), with about 4000 bit errors. SRAM was unaffected. After 120 h annealing, system B recovered; system A and the EEPROM did not. Power draw was stable at about 283-289 mA. Commercial CCD camera images were visibly degraded (Sec V, qualitative only).
q.Q7: None of (1)-(4) as an algorithm. It supplies the empirical grounding for a per-robot cumulative TID budget: COTS electronics are fine to about 100 Gy and fail at about 130-280 Gy. The thesis's 0.1 Gy modeled limit is three orders of magnitude below this, so it must be justified on other grounds (sensors/cameras, detector saturation, conservative design margins, operator policy) or presented as a scaled/normalized budget.

stated_gaps.text: Test sensors, especially CCD cameras, at different dose rates; harden camera
stated_gaps.quote: In the next step we will test the capacity of camera at different dose rates, based on the result and analysis, we will design irradiation hardness camera base on the commercial CCD, which can be used in the mobile robot system.

stated_gaps.text: Test batteries, wires, DC-DC modules, sensors
stated_gaps.quote: we would take more tests about robotic components such as sensors, batteries, wires, DC-DC modules for more experimental data.

stated_gaps.text: Failure doses only roughly estimated
stated_gaps.quote: we gave a rough dose value estimation based on the timing of events.

stated_gaps.text: Dose rate higher than nominal because of scatter
stated_gaps.quote: because of the scatter of walls & ground, the actual value was higher than theoretical value.

stated_gaps.text: MOS parts are designed for low dose rates; TID is the main driver
stated_gaps.quote: For the most majority of robot systems, the primary irradiation driver was total ionizing dose (TID)

stated_gaps.text: Failure depends on dose rate and power state, and is partly recoverable by annealing (system B recovered, EEPROM did not). A single fixed scalar Gy budget is therefore a simplification, and failure is gradual (soft errors, then hard failure), which suggests a probabilistic or multi-threshold damage model.

thesis_relevance: The empirical anchor for treating cumulative dose as a hard, non-renewable per-robot resource. Failure thresholds of about 100-280 Gy for COTS control electronics mean the thesis must explain or rescale its 0.1 Gy budget and could cite this paper for heterogeneous budgets, since different components and robots have different tolerances.

title: Gu, Kuba, Chen, Du, Yang, Knoll, Yang 2023 - Safe multi-agent reinforcement learning for multi-robot control (MACPO / MAPPO-Lagrangian), Artificial Intelligence 319, 103905

q.Q1: Per-agent constraint on expected discounted cumulative cost (CMDP style), not an almost-sure hard budget. Eq. 1: 'J_j^i(pi) = E[sum_t gamma^t C_j^i(s_t, a_t^i)] <= c_j^i', with costs 'C_j^i : S x A^i -> R' and 'every agent i has m^i cost functions' (Sec 3). MACPO 'reaches safety via hard constraints and backtracking line search, while MAPPO-Lagrangian maintains a rather soft safety awareness' (Sec 5.1.2). The guarantee holds during training iterations, in expectation: 'satisfaction of safety constraints at every iteration' (Abstract). Bounds are task-level: 0.2, 1, 5, 10, 30, 2.5, 0.1 (Table A.7). The costs are collisions and proximity, not dose.
q.Q3: No. Costs are emitted by the environment and learned through cost critics (GAE cost advantages). There is no belief over a hazard source and no pessimistic prediction.
q.Q4: Multi-agent here means body-part or joint controllers of a single robot (e.g. Ant 2x4, 4x2, 8x1; ShadowHand 2x6 to 12x1). The formalism allows heterogeneous per-agent thresholds c_j^i, and the sequential update protects other agents' constraints: 'each individual agent has to not only consider its own safety constraints ... but also consider the safety constraints of others' (Sec 1). The experiments do not test unequal per-agent bounds or risk allocation.
q.Q5: Constrained Markov game. Theory: a safe multi-agent policy iteration with monotonic improvement and constraint satisfaction (Theorem 1), extending HATRPO's sequential updates. Algorithms: MACPO (trust region, dual, conjugate gradient, backtracking, recovery step) and MAPPO-L (PPO-clip plus Lagrange multipliers). Benchmarks: Safe MAMuJoCo, Safe MARobosuite and Safe MAIG. Results (curves only): both methods satisfy constraints while MAPPO, IPPO and HAPPO violate them. 'the performance (in terms of reward) of MAPPO-Lagrangian is better than of MACPO'. HAPPO's reward was never exceeded (Sec 5.1.2).
q.Q7: (1): partial in the generic sense. A per-agent cumulative cost constraint exists, but it is an expected, discounted constraint enforced at the policy level, not a per-episode almost-sure budget enforced by an action mask. (2): no. (3): no. (4): partial. The formalism handles inter-agent coupling of constraints and could hold unequal thresholds, but there is no withdrawal or risk sharing. Its reported soft-constraint failure modes support the thesis's finding that MAPPO-L was not suitable.

stated_gaps.text: MAPPO-L is a soft constraint method with delayed reaction and learning-rate sensitivity
stated_gaps.quote: Since MAPPO-L is a soft constraint algorithm, when a safety violation happens, there is a delay to ensure safety, unlike MACPO, which can ensure hard constraints to achieve safety; MAPPO-L is also sensitive to the learning rate.

stated_gaps.text: Stricter constraints reduce reward (conservatism)
stated_gaps.quote: with the stricter safety constraints, the reward performance of MACPO decreases.

stated_gaps.text: Primal-dual methods weak on reward in single-agent safe RL
stated_gaps.quote: Although these methods achieve impressive performance in terms of safety, their performance in terms of reward is poor [39].

stated_gaps.text: Guarantees require small, restrictive policy updates, and the practical algorithm approximates them
stated_gaps.quote: These two properties hold under the condition that only restrictive policy updates are made

stated_gaps.text: Approximation can produce infeasible policies, which need a recovery step
stated_gaps.quote: it is possible that an infeasible policy will be generated.

stated_gaps.text: Constraints are expected discounted costs, so a single episode can violate them. No partial observability of the hazard, no belief-dependent cost, no non-renewable per-episode budget, no exit feasibility. The 'agents' are joints of one robot, not separate robots with separate budgets.
No author-stated future work section beyond the conclusion's hope
stated_gaps.quote: We believe that our findings will contribute to the rise and applicability of many safe MARL methods for multi-robot control.

thesis_relevance: The standard safe-MARL reference (CMDP per-agent constraints, MAPPO-L). It justifies contrasting the thesis's per-episode, belief-based hard shield with expected-cost Lagrangian methods, and its own text documents MAPPO-L's softness and the reward loss under strict bounds that the thesis observed.
